place: Pontic-Caspian steppe, north of the Black and Caspian seas
date: roughly 4,500 to 6,500 years ago (Anthony's c. 4500 to 2500 BCE)
note: The majority view among linguists and archaeologists, strengthened by ancient DNA showing a large movement of steppe ancestry into Europe about 5,000 years ago.
references: Anthony, D. W. (2007) The Horse, the Wheel, and Language: How Bronze-Age Riders from the Eurasian Steppes Shaped the Modern World. Princeton University Press. | Anthony, D. W. and Ringe, D. (2015) The Indo-European homeland from linguistic and archaeological perspectives. Annual Review of Linguistics 1, 199-219. | Haak, W. et al. (2015) Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe. Nature 522, 207-211.

date: roughly 8,000 to 9,500 years ago, with the spread of farming (the authors' approximate range)
note: Links the family's spread to the first farmers; supported by some dated phylogenies, rejected by most specialists because of shared vocabulary for wheels and wagons.
references: Renfrew, C. (1987) Archaeology and Language: The Puzzle of Indo-European Origins. Jonathan Cape. | Bouckaert, R. et al. (2012) Mapping the origins and expansion of the Indo-European language family. Science 337, 957-960.

place: South of the Caucasus (northern Fertile Crescent)
date: about 8,100 years ago for the first split (the authors' estimate)
note: A dated phylogeny places the root south of the Caucasus, with a later branch moving onto the steppe.
references: Heggarty, P. et al. (2023) Language trees with sampled ancestors support a hybrid model for the origin of Indo-European languages. Science 381, eabg0818.

note: Widely accepted: all but one of Austronesian's first-order branches are spoken only on Taiwan.
references: Blust, R. (1999) Subgrouping, circularity and extinction: some issues in Austronesian comparative linguistics. In Zeitoun, E. and Li, P. J.-K. (eds) Selected Papers from the Eighth International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics. Academia Sinica, 31-94. | Gray, R. D., Drummond, A. J. and Greenhill, S. J. (2009) Language phylogenies reveal expansion pulses and pauses in Pacific settlement. Science 323, 479-483.

note: Widely accepted. Bantu is one branch of Atlantic-Congo; the routes of the later spread south and east are debated.
references: Vansina, J. (1995) New linguistic evidence and 'the Bantu expansion'. Journal of African History 36, 173-195. | Grollemund, R. et al. (2015) Bantu expansion shows that habitat alters the route and pace of human dispersals. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 112, 13296-13301.

place: Middle Volga, Kama and the Ural Mountains (approximate)
date: no single agreed date; a dated phylogeny puts the family's first splits several thousand years ago
note: One of two contested views: a homeland in the Volga and Kama region west of the Urals.
references: Honkola, T. et al. (2013) Cultural and climatic changes shape the evolutionary history of the Uralic languages. Journal of Evolutionary Biology 26, 1244-1253.

place: Western Siberia, the Sayan and upper Yenisei area (approximate)
date: spread west from about 4,200 years ago
note: The more recent of the two contested views: a homeland in Siberia, with a spread west to the Volga in the early Metal Age, roughly 4,200 to 3,900 years ago.
references: Grünthal, R., Heyd, V., Holopainen, S., Janhunen, J., Khanina, O., Miestamo, M., Nichols, J., Saarikivi, J. and Sinnemäki, K. (2022) Drastic demographic events triggered the Uralic spread. Diachronica 39(4), 490-524. | Janhunen, J. (2009) Proto-Uralic: what, where, and when? In Ylikoski, J. (ed.) The Quasquicentennial of the Finno-Ugrian Society. Mémoires de la Société Finno-Ougrienne 258, 57-78.

date: about 2,100 years ago for the first split, Bolgar and Common Turkic (95% range 1,500 to 2,800)
note: Broadly agreed for Proto-Turkic itself; its deeper ancestry and any link to Mongolic or other families are disputed.
references: Golden, P. B. (1992) An Introduction to the History of the Turkic Peoples. Harrassowitz. | Savelyev, A. and Robbeets, M. (2020) Bayesian phylolinguistics infers the internal structure and the time-depth of the Turkic language family. Journal of Language Evolution 5(1), 39-53. doi:10.1093/jole/lzz010

place: Upper and middle Yellow River basin, northern China
date: roughly 5,900 to 7,200 years ago (the two studies' estimates)
note: Supported by two dated phylogenies; an alternative places the homeland further south-west, in Sichuan or north-east India.
references: Zhang, M., Yan, S., Pan, W. and Jin, L. (2019) Phylogenetic evidence for Sino-Tibetan origin in northern China in the Late Neolithic. Nature 569, 112-115. | Sagart, L. et al. (2019) Dated language phylogenies shed light on the ancestry of Sino-Tibetan. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 116, 10317-10322.

place: Horn of Africa and the Red Sea hills
date: more than 10,000 years ago, by Ehret's reckoning possibly much earlier
note: Five of the six branches are spoken only in Africa; very old and very uncertain.
references: Ehret, C. (1995) Reconstructing Proto-Afroasiatic (Proto-Afrasian): Vowels, Tone, Consonants, and Vocabulary. University of California Press. | Ehret, C., Keita, S. O. Y. and Newman, P. (2004) The origins of Afroasiatic. Science 306, 1680-1681.

date: more than 10,000 years ago, linked by Militarev to the Natufian
note: Rests on reconstructed farming words; a minority view.
references: Militarev, A. (2002) The prehistory of a dispersal: the Proto-Afrasian (Afroasiatic) farming lexicon. In Bellwood, P. and Renfrew, C. (eds) Examining the Farming/Language Dispersal Hypothesis. McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research, 135-150.

place: West Africa, perhaps the inland Niger region
date: probably more than 10,000 years ago; no agreed date
note: The most uncertain of all: Glottolog does not accept Niger-Congo as a proven family and lists Atlantic-Congo, Mande, Dogon, Ijoid and others separately.
references: Williamson, K. and Blench, R. (2000) Niger-Congo. In Heine, B. and Nurse, D. (eds) African Languages: An Introduction. Cambridge University Press, 11-42. | Güldemann, T. (2018) Historical linguistics and genealogical language classification in Africa. In Güldemann, T. (ed.) The Languages and Linguistics of Africa. De Gruyter Mouton, 58-444.

place: Gulf Plains of north-west Queensland, Australia
date: roughly 6,000 years ago (the authors' approximate estimate)
note: From a dated phylogeography of the family; Pama-Nyungan covers most of Australia.
references: Bouckaert, R. R., Bowern, C. and Atkinson, Q. D. (2018) The origin and expansion of Pama-Nyungan languages across Australia. Nature Ecology and Evolution 2, 741-749.

note: Argues that Proto-Uto-Aztecan speakers were maize farmers who spread north.
references: Hill, J. H. (2001) Proto-Uto-Aztecan: a community of cultivators in central Mexico? American Anthropologist 103, 913-934.

place: South-western United States, southern Great Basin
note: Argues from plant and animal names for a homeland of foragers in the south-west United States.
references: Fowler, C. S. (1983) Some lexical clues to Uto-Aztecan prehistory. International Journal of American Linguistics 49, 224-257.

place: Central coast and highlands of Peru
note: Broadly agreed: the deepest split, between Quechua I and II, lies in central Peru, far from the later Inca centre at Cusco.
references: Torero, A. (1964) Los dialectos quechuas. Anales Científicos de la Universidad Agraria 2, 446-478. | Adelaar, W. F. H. with Muysken, P. C. (2004) The Languages of the Andes. Cambridge University Press.
